maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to be able to announce to the house that an agreement has been signed with the government of Ontario respecting the development of hydro power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river. I now table two copies of the agreement which will of course have to be submitted for approval both by parliament and by the legislature of Ontario. As hon. members will have ample opportunity to consider its provisions at a later date, I will make only a brief statement now as to its general form and purposes.
The agreement with Ontario has been concluded in the expectation that the United States will not participate in the seaway project, and it has been drawn up on the understanding that the navigation works will be undertaken by the federal government and will be entirely within Canada. It contemplates that Ontario will undertake the power development concurrently with an appropriate agency in the United States.
In such circumstances it is desirable that a firm agreement exist between Canada and Ontario in order that Canadian treaty obligations be fulfilled and that other interests in Canada should be safeguarded.
The undertakings on behalf of Ontario are broadly to develop the power resources of the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river concurrently with an appropriate authority in the United States in accordance with the plan known as the "controlled single stage project (238-242)". This
is the same plan as was advanced and made part of the great lakes-St. Lawrence basin agreement of 1941 between Canada and the United States. However, the agreement provides that this plan may be modified as may be agreed upon between Canada and Ontario.
The Canadian government, for its part, undertakes to do all in its power to obtain the approval of the international joint commission to an application to be made by Ontario in an acceptable form for authority from that international body to construct the necessary works. Under the boundary waters treaty of 1909 this approval would be necessary since the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river is a boundary water. Canada's undertaking in this respect is qualified, however, to the extent that its action must be consistent with its obligations under the boundary waters treaty and that regard must be had for all Canadian interests in the St. Lawrence river.
Some of the other more important provisions may be enumerated briefly:
1. Canada will transfer to Ontario the administration of such lands belonging to Canada as are required for the project, and Ontario will pay compensation for these except for lands or property forming part of the existing canal system.
2. Ontario will transfer to Canada the administration of such lands belonging to Ontario as are specified by Canada as being required for works to carry a deep waterway in the international rapids section.
3.	Ontario will establish a commission to safeguard and enhance scenic beauty and historic associations in the section to whatever extent may be appropriate.
It is recognized that before all the arrangements are consummated, as contemplated in this agreement, the great lakes-St. Lawrence basin agreement of 1941 between Canada and the United States may be approved by congress and by parliament. In that event, it would be the intention of the government to reconsider with the government of Ontario the terms of the agreement signed today and to modify them in recognition of the arrangements that would then exist between Canada and the United States with respect to the seaway project.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement with respect to the security measures that have to be taken in connection with defence contracts. The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) spoke in the debate on the address on Wednesday, November 28, of this matter, which is of general concern, and about which I think hon. members might wish to have a statement from the government. It has to do with the problem of safeguarding secret information in industries engaged on defence production.
The hon. member referred to the case of a Mr. George R. Jackson who was recently released from employment by the A. V. Roe Company. Mr. Jackson's case is currently being reviewed and I do not intend to deal with it now. It is the general problem about which I wish to say something.
I think the hon. member for York West has done a service in bringing this matter forward in the serious way he did. The government has to deal with a lot of difficult and unpleasant problems in the conditions of today and of these one of the most difficult, and certainly one of the most unpleasant, is trying to assess the reliability of people who deal or may have to deal with vital defence matters.
As a part of our defence program, contracts have to be placed for the production of various types of equipment, and in many cases this involves the use of details of a highly secret character; secrets which in many cases belong as much to other governments as to our own. Now there are people both in this country and outside who are very anxious to obtain such secrets and who are making constant efforts to find out as much about them as they can. It is, accordingly, vital that no risks be taken which can be reasonably avoided with the security of such defence items. The government is responsible for protecting their secrecy in so far as this country is concerned.
For that reason, any company entering into a contract for the production of defence equipment in Canada must agree that it will exclude from access to secret material any persons about whose reliability the government has any serious doubt. This means that in cases where an individual's background, particularly any associations with communist or pro-communist organizations, or his present associations or even, in some cases, some instability or other qualities of character


raise doubts as to the security of secret matters placed in his hands, then that person must not be allowed access to any secret or vital defence items. It is not possible to give the individual the benefit of the doubt. Reliability for security is not the sort of thing about which conclusive proof one way or the other is usually possible. Sometimes it is, but more often it is a matter of judgment based on all the information that is available. Where the national security is involved, the government simply cannot take the position that defence secrets are to be available to everyone against whom a cut and dried case cannot be made.
The reliability of the overwhelming majority of industrial employees in Canada is beyond doubt. In the case of the few who cannot be said with certainty to be reliable, the government has always to consider two things: the need to avoid doing any injury to an individual and the protection of material vital to the security of this country.
In cases where it is considered that the security of secret material might be endangered by giving a particular individual access to it, the company employing him is informed that such access cannot be allowed. The company is not instructed to dismiss him. I want particularly to emphasize this because there have been statements to the contrary both in the Jackson case and on other occasions. Neither the Department of Defence Production nor any other agency of the government has instructed a company to dismiss an employee for security reasons. A decision that a person should not be entrusted with secret information is not a decision that he is disloyal, and it does not mean that he should be dismissed. It simply means what I have said-that he should not have access to secret information.
There are usually positions in a plant that do not involve security, and transfers to them can be made. It may happen that in some plants which are engaged wholly on defence work such transfers are impossible, for one reason or another. In those cases the company is faced with the choice of releasing the individual or giving up its contract. These are the most difficult cases to handle. It may be that in all instances companies have not done their utmost to find means of making transfers. The importance of always doing so is being brought to their attention. Employers should always try to avoid dismissals if at all possible. They have a duty not to increase the difficulties or disabilities of persons whose only misfortune is that their

reliability is open to question. It is very important that such persons should not be branded as disloyal.
What I want to make clear, however, is that the decision of the government is solely whether it can or cannot risk the security of some vital matter by allowing a particular person to have access to it.- It is up to the employing company to decide what to do about the particular employees who cannot be allowed access to the secret material.
I have dealt thus far with the nature of the problem and the character of the task that the government attempts to perform in protecting the security of defence production. The procedure in handling the matter is also a problem.
The hon. member for York West suggested, as others commenting on this matter have suggested, that there should be a board or panel to hear representations from individuals before decisions are taken as to their reliability for security. This suggestion appeals to most fair-minded people because it seems to accord with the general principles on which we proceed in dealing with charges or claims against a man in criminal or civil law and in other instances. There are, however, particular considerations that have to be weighed on the other side.
In the first place, the assessment of the reliability of a person does not necessarily, or even usually, involve anything that could be regarded as "charges" against him. Decisions on reliability are taken every day in the public service and, indeed, in business and in almost every sort of organization. Most hon. members will at one time or another have been in a position where they have to decide whether they could or could not rely on a particular person in some important matter.
The only thing that distinguishes the cases I am talking about is that in defence production, and more particularly in the development stage of defence production, some methods and processes are of enormous importance and their betrayal could do injury to the whole nation. Reliability is more critically important than in most other circumstances. The question at issue is not guilt or innocence of some particular charge. The sole question is whether a certain person can or cannot be entrusted' with secret defence material. It would give a completely false atmosphere to the matter if it were assumed that reliability can somehow be put beyond doubt by meeting formal charges-or indeed, that reliability cannot be brought into doubt except on the basis of formal charges. Assessment of character may be the only consideration in
Defence Production-Security Measures some instances. That is not a matter of charges, or of trial or of proof. It is a matter of judgment.
A second consideration to be borne in mind is that in dealing with reliability in defence production we are not in the realm of what have come to be called "human rights" and "fundamental freedoms". There is no human right or fundamental freedom involved. No person has a right of access to secret defence items, and no man's freedom is infringed when he is denied such access. In a particular case a company may decide that it has no place where it can employ a man who cannot be given access to defence matters. In such a case the man's job becomes involved. Where that is so, it is always possible for a company to ask that a case be reviewed to see if the decision cannot be reversed, and the government is always ready to make such a review. But in the last analysis, the question for the government and the question it must decide is whether it is or is not satisfied that there would be no risk to the security of some secret material or process by letting a certain person have access to it. No outside panel or board can take that responsibility. No matter how much the government might like to be relieved of this very unpleasant duty no government would have the right to shift to others the responsibility for the security of our defence secrets.
There is a further consideration of an entirely different order that is also relevant. It is that hearings could and probably would compromise our general security precautions. Some of the people about whose access to secret material we have to be most concerned operate in the interests of an organization that is skilfully and tightly bound together. This organization acts with a ruthlessness and a readiness to sacrifice its own followers, which we find it almost impossible to appreciate. It is only by careful, long continued and patient work that means have been established by our police forces of getting information about the operations of this organization. The organization would be more than ready to precipitate hearings involving their own followers, even if it meant the personal ruin of those individuals, if the hearings would lay bare the sources of information that the police have established. If hearings were held, the information as to the background or other considerations causing doubt about an individual would have to be revealed. I do not see how a "hearing" could be regarded as serving any purpose if that were not so. More than that, it would be argued that the validity of such information or the grounds for doubt could not be assessed nor could any "charges" be properly refuted unless the kind and sources

North Atlantic Treaty
of information were disclosed, the informants questioned, and so forth. If that were done in even two or three instances, they might be sufficient to nullify, in very short order, such security defences as we have been able to build up after years of painstaking effort. The well-organized opponents of our way of life would be more than ready to sacrifice a good many of their supporters to gain the kind of information that hearings would inevitably reveal.
For the reasons I have given, the government has thus far taken the view that no one has a valid claim to be given a hearing before he is denied access to secret defence material or processes of defence production. It has considered that a system of hearings should not be instituted. This means, of course, that the responsibility of the government is the greater to see thht every case is carefully assessed and that no decisions as to the reliability of an individual are lightly taken. They are not lightly taken. Moreover, the cases can always be re-examined and the government will have no reluctance about reversing an original decision if further review suggests that it can safely be reversed. This whole matter is, however, distorted and seen in a false light, if it is confused with loyalty and thought of in terms of specific, provable or disprovable charges. You can doubt the reliability of a man for the security of some vital defence matter without considering him to be disloyal. You can continue to doubt no matter how much he argues or protests.
The problem that is thrust on the government of assessing the reliability of employees in defence industries, and occasionally of deciding in some case that reliability is uncertain, is not a pleasant one. In the present state of things it is, however, an unavoidable one. It is the government itself which is and must be answerable for the security of our defence secrets. The government is, however, fully aware of the importance of ensuring in so far as possible that no injury is done to any individual through the decisions that must be taken. Security procedures are constantly under review, and if they can be improved, the government will always be ready to make the improvements and will always welcome and seriously consider constructive suggestions to that end.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxion (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: STATEMENT FOLLOWING MEETING OF COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is usual for a statement to be made in this house when a minister returns from an international conference of major importance. The eighth

meeting of the North Atlantic council concluded at Rome last week. This was the first meeting attended by the supreme commander, General Eisenhower, and the meeting met under the inspiration of his personality. At the conclusion of its business, the council of twelve nations agreed on a statement to be made public. Because of the nature of the meeting and of the business transacted there, and also because my colleagues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), as well as myself, have not yet had an opportunity to report to the government, it is not possible to go into greater detail than is contained in this statement. For the convenience of hon. members, however, I should like to table a copy of the statement that was issued in Rome.
Canada's contribution to European defence-

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minisier of Naiional Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while during these last two weeks I have been out of sight here, apparently, judging from Hansard. I have not been entirely forgotten. I feel that at this time the house would expect from me a word of personal explanation of matters arising out of press reports published in my absence. I have read the Hansard references and most of the press reports, but I do not intend to enter into details-that has already been covered here-and I certainly do not mean to indulge in any recriminations. My real purpose is to assure the house that I had no intention of making announcements in Europe of new policies of which hon. members had not been informed in this chamber.
I made references to accommodation for our troops and to airfields, and no doubt those matters were much less familiar to some hon. members and members of the press than I had supposed; and it may be that there was some justification for a feeling that some kind of announcement of new policy had been made. I am sorry indeed if any answers I gave to questions created the impression that I was making important announcements outside the house. I have always tried to give the house all possible information on defence matters and, when the house is in session, to make all statements of major new developments and new policies in this chamber.
On looking over the reports, I think I can understand how the misunderstanding arose. As hon. members had been informed, the decision to dispatch the 27th Canadian infantry brigade group was not taken until the government had been assured that temporary accommodation was available. That temporary accommodation would have to be

replaced by new accommodation. It is a fact, not a policy, that troops must be housed. As for airfields for the use of our air squadrons, hon. members had already been informed that airfields were not available on the continent, and that pending their availability, Canadian squadrons would be stationed in the United Kingdom at North Luffenham. Consequently, it was known that airfields would have to be provided on the continent.
We knew also that, in accord with the policy that parliament had accepted that Canada should do its share in NATO, we would also have to participate in meeting the costs of infrastructure-to use that horrible expression. To me that appeared to be a statement of a situation, of a condition, of a fact, and not of a policy.
Indeed it was not possible for me to state a new policy because the government had not yet decided upon one; and the government had not yet decided upon policy because the North Atlantic treaty nations concerned had not and have not yet fully worked out an agreement as to precisely how this should be done or how the over-all costs should be shared. That is one of the matters we discussed on the other side and it is a matter that was under active discussion in connection with the Rome meeting, and it is still under the most active consideration at Paris.
There is also the question of working out arrangements for accommodation and other facilities in Germany when the occupation statute is converted into an agreement. This is under consideration by the three occupying powers and the German government today.
Consequently, it is not possible either to announce a policy or to give any details or estimates of the over-all costs that might be involved. Just as soon as firm arrangements are worked out with the other countries concerned, they will be announced.
Against this background I repeat that I am indeed sorry if any hon. member feels that I was discussing new policies of which the house had not been informed and I assure you, sir, I had no such intention. Now that the smoke has cleared from the atmosphere here and elsewhere, I must leave it to hon. members themselves to decide in the light of the real facts whether I did or not.
May I ask the minister if he is in a position to indicate what our commitments are with respect to military installations on the continent?
No. I have just said that I am not.

Then the press report of four or five airdromes and landing fields is incorrect?
North Atlantic Treaty

We will need four or five airfields to furnish our eleven squadrons with flying facilities. We will also need housing accommodation. But how much will be needed, where it will be located or what it will cost, we are in no position to say today.
May I ask the minister this question? Is the construction or purchase to be at the cost of Canada?
Of Canada?
Yes.

I am not in a position to say that. I can go this far and say that part of the cost will form part of the costs that will be shared by all North Atlantic treaty nations in accordance with an agreed formula. Part of it may have to be borne directly by us. Preliminary estimates of the most tentative character would indicate that whichever course is followed would not make much financial difference to us.
Is Canada proceeding at once with the construction of barracks and the construction of airfields in Germany?
We are not in committee.

I cannot go much further than I have gone, Mr. Speaker. We are at present occupying temporary accommodation for the 27th infantry brigade group in Germany. That will have to be relinquished at some future date and we will have to make arrangements for construction of accommodation for the brigade group in Germany. What those arrangements will be, who will do the construction, and how the payments will be made, remains to be worked out not only as between ourselves and the three occupying powers but as between the three occupying powers and Germany.
What about airfields?
Order.

The position with regard to airfields is similar, but there the probability is that all airfields will be located outside Germany and probably in France. Arrangements therefore will have to be made with SHAPE for the location and development of the airfields and the sharing of costs in so far as they are to be shared and then in all probability either through SHAPE or directly with the French government for accommodation.
May I ask the minister whether any request was made that Canada should increase her number of troops in Europe from a brigade to a division?

I am not in a position to discuss that matter on this statement.

subtopic: PLACEMENT SERVICE
PLACEMENT SERVICE
speechtext:
1.	Is the Department of Citizenship and Immigration operating a placement service for immigrants?
2.	Does the national employment service also operate a placement service for immigrants?
3.	Does the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and also the Department of Labour, have officials in the field seeking places of employment for immigrants?
4.	If so, how many officials, and in what areas?
5.	What is the division of responsibility between the two departments in placing immigrants?
6.	Do the departments above-mentioned absorb the cost of movement of immigrants from the point of entry into Canada to the point of employment?
7.	Does the Department of Citizenship and Immigration or the Department of Labour seek co-operation of or consult with provincial governments in placing immigrants?

subtopic: PLACEMENT SERVICE
speechtext:
1.	The Department of Citizenship and Immigration operates a settlement service for the purpose of locating and developing suitable opportunities for immigrants who come to Canada to settle on farms, or establish small businesses of their own. The department also helps immigrants secure employment, and handles applications from employers for immigrant workers.
2.	The facilities of the national employment service are available to, and used by, immigrant workers. Employment office officials keep in close touch with the hostels and assist in referring immigrant workers to prospective employers.
3.	See answers to Nos. 1 and 2.
4.	The immigration branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has one settlement officer at each of the following locations:	Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina,
Winnipeg, London, Toronto, Montreal, Quebec and Halifax. These officers are assisted, as required, by immigration inspectors and other staff of the immigration branch throughout the dominion.
In national employment offices certain placement officials have the duty of keeping in close contact with employers in their area in order that they may advise the employers where workmen can be obtained to meet their needs. The total number of placement officers

in the national employment service varies, depending upon the season of the year. When the claim load is great the duties of the placement officers change in some instances and the staff of the unemployment insurance commission works as a unit as between duties applying to unemployment insurance and placement work. The total number of men and women engaged on placement work in Canada varies from approximately 900 to 1,200.
5.	The whole immigration movement is primarily the responsibility of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. This involves development of settlement opportunities in Canada, recruitment and selection overseas, admission, assistance in becoming established, and integration into Canadian society with attainment of full Canadian citizenship as the objective.
As stated in the answer to No. 1, the settlement service of the immigration branch, Department of Citizenship and Immigration, locates and develops farm and business opportunities. The national employment service places immigrants brought in under group or bulk movements to meet general labour shortages, or the needs of employers who apply to the labour department for the admission of a number of workers. The facilities of both departments are available to the large body of immigrants, should they be seeking employment, thus placing a widespread placement or settlement service at their disposal. The whole operation is recognized as one which can best be carried out by the closest possible co-operation between the two departments. The facilities of the national employment service are available to immigrants as well as other residents of Canada.
6.	The department of citizenship has been authorized to provide for the absorption of the cost of inland rail transportation west of Winnipeg for immigrants who come to Canada under the assisted passage loan scheme who remain for one year in the class of employment for which they were selected.
The Department of Labour absorbs the cost of inland transportation for immigrant domestics, and farm workers who are brought forward in group movements.
7.	Yes.

maintopic: REPORTED CRUELTY IN TREATMENT OF CANADIAN MISSIONARIES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED CRUELTY IN TREATMENT OF CANADIAN MISSIONARIES
speechtext:
I should like
to direct an inquiry to the Prime Minister, notice of which I gave him earlier in the day. Is he in a position to say what official word has been received as to the reportedly harsh and cruel treatment being accorded to Canadian missionaries in red China?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPORTED CRUELTY IN TREATMENT OF CANADIAN MISSIONARIES
speechtext:
Unfortunately, I am not in a
position to give any information about the events that have been reported in the press as having taken place over the last two or three days. It will be remembered that on April 16 the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made a statement in the house regarding the situation of five Canadian sisters of the Immaculate Conception who had been arrested by the Chinese communists in Canton. It was at that time hoped that representations made by the United Kingdom charge d'affaires in Peking on their behalf as well as on behalf of other Canadian citizens held in custody would bring an improvement in their condition. Well, we are informed that no such improvement occurred, and the charge d'affaires made further strong representations to the Peking government on September 1, and on September 10, when parliament was not in session, the department issued a press release. Perhaps it might help if for the convenience of hon. members I tabled a copy of the press release containing the information that was available up to that time.
During the past two days news services have carried stories of the formal prosecution and sentencing of the five nuns at so-called public trials on December 1. According to these reports, Sister St. Alphonse du Redempteur, (Antoinette Couvrette, bom at Ste. Dorothee, Quebec) and Sister Marie-Germaine (Germaine Gravel of St. Pasteur, Quebec) were sentenced to five years' imprisonment. Sister Ste. Foy (Elizabeth Lemire of La Baie du Febvre, Quebec), Sister St. Victor (Germaine Tanguay, born in Acton Vale, Quebec) and Sister Ste. Germaine (Imelda Laperriere of Pont Rouge, Quebec) were ordered to be deported from China. The Canadian government has no official confirmation as yet of these reports.
Inquiries of the Ministry
We know that the five nuns have been in a Canton prison since March of this year when they were arrested on what was considered to be the fantastic charge of being responsible for the deaths between October 14, 1949, and January 14, 1951, of over two thousand children who had been receiving care in their orphanage. Their arrests followed upon Canton newspaper stories and the demands of women's organizations that they be severely punished for the maltreatment and murder of children. It may be true that quite a large number of children have died at the orphanage, but the Chinese authorities chose to ignore the fact that the majority of the children brought to the sisters were already ailing and beyond hope of recovery when accepted by them. The sisters consistently accepted all children brought to them for help, whatever their condition was at that time, and no matter what were their chances for survival.
As I have already said, no official report regarding the trial of the five nuns has yet been received in Canada, and it is possible that it may be difficult to secure any accurate and reliable information about the so-called trials. I can assure the house that everything possible will be done to help these unfortunate sisters without bringing more harm on them or other Canadians who are being detained by the Chinese communists at this time. I think that the order of expulsion may be perhaps the most happy denouement, and it would be unfortunate if anything we said or did brought about, as has happened in the past, revocation of the order of expulsion, or the placing of difficulties in the quitting of the country.
The house will be shocked and indignant at the treatment which has apparently been meted out to a group of missionaries who for years have consecrated their lives to the care of orphan children in China; but it will be at the same time sensitive to the extreme delicacy of the situation and the necessity of avoiding any act or word which may add to their present distress. Within the next few days we hope to have more definite information on the whereabouts of the three nuns whose expulsion has been ordered, and on the situation of the two who have been sentenced to terms of imprisonment. We are hopeful that we may, through the British authorities in Hong Kong, be able to get information from and about these nuns, because we presume that they would go through Hong Kong on their way out of the country. I shall naturally keep the house informed of anything that we can regard as accurate in the way of information about them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned last Wednesday we were discussing the question of federal aid to education. That discussion arose out of an answer made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on Tuesday,


November 27, 1951, as recorded at page 1355 of Hansard. I shall return to that question and answer later.
At the outset I wish to say that the question of federal aid is not one in which only a few individuals are concerned. It is one that is of wide concern to all Canadians, generally. It is a question that has been a subject of public discussion, to my personal knowledge, for nearly a quarter of a century. In 1938, as chairman of the educational finance committee of the Canadian teachers federation, I appeared with a committee on behalf of that federation before the Rowell-Sirois commission in this city to place before it arguments in favour of federal aid for education. During that same year teachers' organizations in every province throughout Canada appeared before the commission as it moved across the country. Since that date such national organizations as the trade union congresses, national and provincial organizations of ratepayers and school trustees, national and provincial organizations of home and school clubs, various manufacturers associations and boards of trade, and home owners associations throughout the country have all lent their support to federal aid for education. The matter is one of too much concern to too many people in Canada to be peremptorily laid aside and dismissed without any further consideration by any one person, even if that one person is the very highly respected Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent).
It is generally agreed that it is the right of every Canadian child to secure the best in education, consistent with his need and capacity, that the resources of the state can provide. That is accepted today as the birthright of Canadian children. It is also agreed that such an opportunity cannot be afforded to Canadian children so long as we continue to finance our schools as we do today. There can be no justification in a democracy for providing at public expense better educational opportunities for the future citizens of one section of the country than are provided for those of another part of the country. Since our children are born as Canadian children, as Canadian citizens and not provincial or municipal citizens, the educational opportunity which is afforded to any Canadian child in any municipality in Canada is a matter of importance to the whole of Canada.
It is true that the control of education was delegated by the terms of the British North America Act to the provincial authorities, and in my opinion it was delegated to them for two reasons. First, there was the necessity of safeguarding the racial and religious

interests of the minorities. Without the safeguarding of these racial and religious interests, confederation would have been impossible. The second reason, which I think carried weight at that time, was that in 1867 there was no widespread belief in this country that education was a matter of great national importance or that education was of importance outside the provinces.
The necessity of safeguarding the racial and religious interests of minorities is as great today as it was in 1867. Nevertheless it has been proven conclusively over the years, and beyond any shadow of doubt, that federal support can be given to education without any interference with the rights of the provinces in this matter. Our most recent grants-in-aid to universities are being given with the distinct understanding that the federal government will in no way interfere with the freedom of our universities nor the right of the provinces to exercise their constitutional authority over these same universities. The federal government's magnificent support of education for the men and women of world war II is only another example of federal aid to education given within the terms of our constitution and without interference with provincial rights.
The need for federal aid for education at the elementary and secondary school levels goes much deeper into our national life than appears on the surface. It involves more than the provision of equal educational opportunities for Canadian children, important as that may be. It touches the conditions of home life in our communities. Today there are tens of thousands of Canadians, particularly in the low income groups, who require houses at a cost that they can afford to pay. The federal government recognized this fact in the terms of our national housing legislation. Provision was made therein whereby the federal government might enter into agreements with provinces and municipalities for the building of low rental houses. Even with the federal government's generous offer to bear 75 per cent of the cost and of the deficits of those houses, that has been a failure. So far as I can find out, not one single house has yet been built in Ontario under the terms of that legislation.
Provincial authorities in Ontario tell me that municipalities are reluctant to have low rental houses built within their boundaries1. Why? Because working class people as a rule still raise comparatively large families-surely something to be encouraged rather than discouraged. Large families mean heavy taxes for education, and as long as municipalities and real estate in municipalities are required to carry the larger share of that cost you will
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy have municipalities objecting to the building of low rental houses within their boundaries. Because we get no low rental houses, families today are forced to live in crowded and often unsanitary conditions, to live under conditions that discourage the raising of families and have a very undesirable effect upon those who are being raised. Federal aid for education is actually becoming a matter of more and more vital importance to the welfare of Canada as a nation. It is too important to warrant its rejection by the federal government on a mere technicality.
May I point out further that our neighbours to the south are faced with a similar constitutional problem, but they have in large measure solved that problem. The fact that the individual states in the union have constitutional control over education has not prevented their federal government from making generous grants-in-aid to education at every level. Their experience has shown that these grants can be made without impairing the constitutional rights of the states over education. Surely it is time that we in Canada took an adult view of this matter.
Returning to the question and answer which provoked this debate, the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), which will be found reported at page 1355 of Hansard of November 27, was as follows:
Has the government received from the Winnipeg school board, and perhaps from others, a request that consideration be given to extending federal aid to education generally?
The answer of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to be found on the same page, was as follows:
While I have the responsibility as the head of the government I would have to ask my colleagues to join with me in refusing to consider such a request.
When I spoke last Wednesday I did not have the exact wording of that answer before me and at the time I was inclined to agree with the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) when he said that the Prime Minister's reply applied only to a specific question with regard to the Winnipeg school board. The question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre went beyond the specific question raised by the Winnipeg school board. It embraced others and asked whether consideration was being given to extending federal aid to education generally. It was in answer to that question that the Prime Minister stated that as long as he was leader of this government he would have to ask his colleagues to refuse to give consideration to that matter.

Production, manufacturing, processing and distribution of dairy products in some 2,000 dairy plants provide the direct or indirect livelihood of 17 per cent of Canada's total population. This is indicated in another fine little booklet of the national dairy council entitled "What is Best for Canada".
Soil fertility maintenance will always be a "must" for every wise people and government. In Canada this truth applies with

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
cogent force. Many, many farms have been abandoned in Canada-far, far too many, and especially in Ontario and the maritime provinces. Great numbers of farms in Canada have simply become worn out. When we contrast that situation with the way in which the fertility and yielding capacity of soil in most parts of Great Britain have been preserved down through the centuries, we must find cause for complete shame in Canada.
Far, far too many of our farmers in Canada merely mine the soil. This is particularly true through the western provinces. The mechanization of our farms is rapidly displacing the horse, with his requirements of fibre-restoring pasture and his natural return of nutrients to the soil. This is a matter which has been given too little attention in calculating policy for Canada.
Over a great percentage of this country erosion by wind and water is taking place at an alarming rate. Surely we do not have to wait until this nation becomes a pile of rocks before the people in responsible positions take common-sense action, and do something about it.
As reported in the Alberta wheat pool budget of November 23, 1951, the research laboratory of the experimental farm at Swift Current points out that the weight of an inch of water falling upon an acre of soil is close to 110 tons. The drops falling upon the bare soil splash about 22 J tons of clay or clay loam. The run-off can carry away a substantial weight of this soil to where it becomes non-available. From the 1936-1948 progress report of the division of field husbandry, soils and agricultural engineering of the central experimental farm, Ottawa, we learn the following as to the effect of manure on water erosion of soil:
Results on soil and water runoff on summerfallow and corn plots on a 10 per cent slope are available from two series, one of which received 16 tons of manure per acre at the time the plots were established in 1944 and again in the fall of 1947, and the other has received no manure.
The average loss per acre for a cropping season during the period 1945 to 1948 inclusive on the manured summerfallow plot was 31-9 tons of soil and 228-2 tons of water, as compared with 381 tons of soil and 298-5 tons of water on a plot similar except that no manure was applied. Where com was grown, the runoff was 31-1 tons of soil and 289-3 tons of water on the manured plot as compared with 39-3 tons of soil and 319-8 tons of water where no manure was applied.
Manure improves the physical condition- of the soil favouring greater absorption of water, and consequently less erosion occurs.
The dairy cow is the greatest rehabilitating agent available to man. Let us never forget that. There are three main means of rehabilitating soils: first, through artificial fertilizers;
IMr. Blackmore.]
second, through green manure by the plowing under of legumes, sweet clover, red clover and the like; and third, through livestock manure. Barnyard manure from cattle is in every way the best means of rehabilitating soil. I should like to refer to a national dairy council of Canada report based on experiments and observations at our experimental farm. The article reads:
Farmyard manure constitutes the most valuable by-product of the farm. During the last war the Department of Agriculture estimated that 114,147,000 tons of manure exclusive of bedding materials are produced each year by the livestock in Canada. On the basis of average chemical analyses of the excrement from various species of animals, the nutrients in the total manure produced would be equivalent to 3,353,550 tons of sulphate of ammonia, 1,024,145 tons of superphosphate (20 per cent P205) and 1,137,825 tons of muriate of potash.
In addition to these potential nutrients manure adds large quantities of valuable organic matter to the soil, thereby improving the tilth of both light and heavy soils.
The approximate amount of nutrients in a mixture of fresh manure from the common species of farm animals is 10 pounds of nitrogen per ton of manure, 5 pounds of phosphoric acid and 10 pounds of potash. One mature milk cow would produce about 1 ton of manure a month. At this rate milk cows in Canada last year produced over 43 million tons of manure of a fertilizer potential in terms of soil nutrients of 216,540 tons of nitrogen, 108,270 tons of phosphoric acid and 216,540 tons of potash.
What is the best combination of means of rehabilitating soils? Experiments have been *conducted for a good many years in Canada in an effort to determine whether or not artificial fertilizers can replace manure, whether artificial fertilizers together with green manure can sufficiently rebuild soils, or whether it becomes necessary to have barnyard manure, and just what is the result of combining the three one way and another. An experiment has been conducted in Lethbridge in which hon. members will be interested. It has to do with sugar beets, wheat and alfalfa. I should like to quote a page from "Silver Sunshine", a document published by Canadian Sugar Factories Limited. It is the fall edition, 1951. I read from page 5, as follows:
Each plot consists of four fertility treatments: 1. Barnyard manure and mineral fertilizer; 2. barnyard manure only; 3. mineral fertilizer only; 4. no additions.
The barnyard manure is applied and ploughed in the fall of the year prior to the first year beets at the rate of 30 tons per acre. This manure taken from the livestock barns and feeding corrals is piled for a year to kill weed seeds, before it is spread on the plots. Until the last few years, triple superphosphate was drilled in with the beet seed at 100 pounds per acre on the plots receiving mineral fertilizer. Due to the shortage of this fertilizer, 11-48-0 is now used at the same rate.

I do not know that the situation needs to be more serious than that.
Unless we take steps at once, and the right kind of steps, to aid our dairymen, Canadians will rue this day through which we are passing for a long time to come. Possibly they shall rue it when the means of remedying the situation will have been largely removed from their control.
What are the causes of this dangerous decline? The first cause is the low cost of margarine. The second reason for this decline is the high cost of butter. As everyone knows, butter has risen rapidly in price. On October 17, 1951, basis Toronto delivered, the price was 69 cents per pound, according to figures provided me by the national dairy council. The third reason is the low cost of vegetable oils, to which I have already referred. Prices in the United States market for crude vegetable oils on October 16 were as follows: cottonseed oil, 14-5 cents; soybean oil, 13| cents; peanut oil, 16| cents; coconut oil, 14 cents. In February, just a few months earlier, the prices for these same products were as follows: 24J cents; 21J cents; 27 cents and 24J cents. This shows how rapidly the price of these vegetable oils is going down, while the price of butter must unquestionably go up or we shall not produce butter.
The fourth reason is a lack of tariff protection against incoming vegetable oils. Oils, including copra, enter into Canada from British preference countries and certain other of the principal edible oil exporting countries in the world entirely free of tariff duty. Most oils from the United States used in substitutes pay only 10 per cent tariff duty, or approximately 1J cents per pound at today's prices. This information was provided by the national dairy council.
The fifth reason is the rapid increase of percentage use of vegetable oils in margarine, 1950 to 1951. They have come to use more and more of this vegetable oil in the manufacture of a given weight of margarine. As the percentage of oils used increases, so the margarine becomes cheaper to produce. The percentage of coconut and other vegetable oils,

mostly peanut, used in the manufacture of margarine increased from 10-8 per cent in the January-August period of 1950 to 23-9 per cent of the total in the same period of 1951. This represents an increase of 146-3 per cent in the utilization of coconut and other oils in the first eight months of this year compared with last. Again these figures are supplied by the national dairy council. What is the result? A tremendous growth in the over-all importation of vegetable oils. I have a set of figures which I shall put on Hansard, if it is the will of the house, which reveal the low cost of margarine to retail stores. This set of figures which was prepared by the dairy council is very enlightening.

The question is, what to do? A tariff would naturally tend to force up prices of dairy products substitutes greatly to the distress of consumers. I am opposed to any increased costs to consumers. At this time they are paying all they can possibly stand. Most

We could use an excise tax upon the manufacture of margarine and all substitutes for dairy products. Again this would increase consumer costs. We could use a subsidy on milk and all milk products.

Butter

We could use guarantees of prices of materials entering into production of dairy products, also guarantees of prices and markets for our finished dairy products. We could use quotas to avoid vegetable oils displacing Canadian dairy production. Mr. Speaker, I wish to detain the house for a few minutes on a matter which I think is of interest and importance. But before doing so I wish to take just a minute to put on the record what I found some difficulty in putting on it earlier in the afternoon because at
The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell that time hon. members did not seem to be greatly interested. I was interested in the light-hearted brushing aside by the parliamentary assistant of the words which were, I think, uttered seriously by the finance minister and which were taken seriously by this house last April. I propose to read just a sentence or two from what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) then said, which will indicate what I was not able to indicate owing to the enthusiasm shown an hour and a half ago by those who so valiantly support everything a government member says. This will indicate that the Minister of Finance apparently spoke seriously, and that he gave the house to understand that the various increased costs had been taken care of in his estimates. As reported at page 1801 of Hansard the Minister of Finance said:
The estimates placed before parliament for this year show a reduction of $35 million below last year, despite an increase of more than 10 per cent in salary and wage levels, despite higher materials and construction costs, and despite an increase of nearly $40 million in old age pensions, family allowances, tax rental agreements with provinces, and similar payments that rise automatically with increases in population and the value of production. The numbers of employees engaged in normal government administration are being reduced . . .
And so on. I shall not pursue the matter further, Mr. Speaker, but I just want to reiterate that we had this afternoon, in the answer given to me, what I regard as a rather clever escape or attempt to escape by an utterly irresponsible answer, having regard to what the minister said last April.
I wish to take a few minutes of the time of the house in order to bring to the attention of hon. members some remarks made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) which seemed to me to have been in the highest degree uncalled for, to put it mildly. These remarks were made before the United Nations first of all last January; then further remarks were made a few weeks ago in Paris. At a time when it seems highly desirable to safeguard and nourish common understanding, the minister seems to have gone out of his way to heap criticism on commonwealth statesmen for decisions made by them. Moreover, the line which he took was entirely inconsistent with the line taken at the time by the government of which he is now a member and which at that time he was serving in another capacity.
I shall have to touch on matters which carry the mind back more than a decade; but the excursion into the past, which will be brief, is the minister's responsibility and not mine. I am sorry he is not here today. I have tried to give notice to his parliamentary assistant. I think today is my only
1532

The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell chance to bring this matter before the house. It is a matter which has attracted attention outside of the house, and I consider it to be right and proper that it should be put on the record of the house also.
In a speech last January before the first -political-committee of the United Nations, the minister referred to a certain statement of principles prepared by the so-called "cease-fire" group of which he was a member, and referred to criticisms made 'of this group on the ground that they were, in the minister's words, "in danger of repeating the betrayal of Munich". The minister then went on to use these words:
The tragedy of Munich . . . was not in going there. It might have been better if more governments had been able to accept the responsibilities of being there. The tragedy was in what was done there and our statement of principles did not I think recommend doing anything that meant the betrayal of a people or a principle, nor was it a weak surrender to armed pressure or a naive mis' understanding of a political situation.
Those are the minister's words. Then later the minister referred to
My country which-
In his words:
-was not represented at Munich.
Munich was evidently greatly on the minister's mind because he returned to it again on November 12 before the United Nations in Paris. Here are the words that he then used:
It is always easy to secure peace and a kind of security on the other man's terms. But we know where that can lead-to the humiliation of a Chamberlain or the death of a Mazaryk.
I am not one of those who applauded Munich. I was not satisfied then, and I have never been satisfied since, as to the wisdom of what was done there. I felt deeply the abandonment of the Czechs and the loss of the Skoda works and the Czech divisions. As I said a moment ago, nothing that has happened since has definitely satisfied me of the wisdom of what was done. But notwithstanding my views, it seemed to me that at that time any fair-minded man would feel that the Statesmen who were carrying the appalling responsibility of that time were entitled to sympathy. I have refreshed my memory by rereading the press of that time, and it recalls the tension and the appalling anxiety which was felt by people who had not yet really girded themselves to face war again. We recall the stories of trenches in Hyde Park and all that kind of thing.
Again I say that no man of fairness or common sense should have criticized the decision except in moderate words, and never should have criticized it except as an error of judgment. How different are the words


which I have already read such as "betrayal", "weak surrender" and "naive misunderstanding". I found them to be extremely jarring. The minister knows the meaning of words, and it will not surprise him to know that the dictionary defines "betrayal" as "a treacherous giving up to an enemy". One would have thought that the minister's own difficulties in reaching conclusions in the Korean affair would have prevented him from using language of this kind. For example, I contrast his language with the language of Mr. Eden, who had resigned from the Chamberlain government, who was extremely dubious about Munich but who hailed Munich as at any rate a "respite", who referred to the "unparalleled ordeal" that Chamberlain as prime minister had been through, and who said that the people of England owed him "a measureless debt of gratitude" for his "sincerity and pertinacity". Those were the words of a man who really did not approve of Munich but who understood and sympathized with the appalling responsibility which was carried.
I now return to one other point. The minister referred to Canada not being represented. The clear implication of that reference is that there would have been no "betrayal", no "weak surrender" and no "naive misunderstanding" if only we had been there. You will remember the facts, Mr. Speaker. What are the facts? Was the government of Canada silent? Was it critical or noncommittal as to what happened at Munich? What did Mr. King, Mr. Lapointe and their colleagues say at that time? It is quite clear. It is contained in a cable sent by the then prime minister, Mr. King, immediately after the events of Munich, in the following terms:
Ottawa, September 29, 1938
The Right Honourable Neville Chamberlain,

Prime Minister of Great Britain,
10 Downing Street,
London, England.
The heart of Canada is rejoicing tonight at the success which has crowned your unremitting efforts for peace. May I convey to you the warm congratulations of the Canadian people, and with them, an expression of their gratitude, which is felt from one end of the dominion to the other. My colleagues in the government join with me in unbounded admiration at the service you have rendered mankind. Your achievements in the past month alone will ensure you an abiding and illustrious place among the great conciliators whom the United Kingdom, the British commonwealth of nations and the whole world will continue to honour. On the very brink of chaos, with passions flaming, and armies marching, the voice of reason has found a way out of the conflict which no people in their heart desired, but none seemed able to avert. A turning point in the world's history will be reached if, as we hope, tonight's agreement means a halt

to the mad race of arms, and a new start in building the partnership of all peoples. May you have health and strength to carry your great work to its completion.
W. L. Mackenzie King.
Here is the view expressed by the Canadian government. It is not my view, but it was held by people far more important than I am; by statesmen of Britain, by statesmen of the commonwealth and, as I have just indicated, by the government of Canada. In any event, this cable makes nonsense or mincemeat of the minister's implication that if we had been represented at Munich all might have been different.
However attractive it may be to criticize decisions after the event, I suggest that it is ungenerous and it sometimes has pitfalls.

From 1930 to 1935, when the Tory party was running this country, our workers were compelled to queue up outside city halls to be handed welfare tokens worth $5.60 per week. At night they headed for the Meurling shelter or the breadline. In spite of the high cost of living, do you think that our people would change their present situation? Do you think that our people, in spite of the high cost of living, would exchange their present conditions with high salaries, obviously easy circumstances, social legislation which our government can be proud of, such as family allowances, old age pensions, blind persons' pensions or unemployment insurance, for the misery they underwent during the days of the Tory regime, between 1930 and 1935? At that time our country was going hungry under mountains of wheat which it had no money to buy. In every walk of life, from the lumberjack in the forest to the highly-paid workers of our factories, large and small, the standard of living has risen in such a way as to cause them to forget the increased cost of living. We therefore hear few complaints levelled at the present administration,. On the contrary the people are happy to possess the leader, the cabinet, and the administration they now enjoy. A few days ago, I visited a sick relative at the Montreal Radium Institute. At that time, this institute was celebrating the twenty-fifth anniversary of its foundation and I was grieved to see the difficult conditions under which the sick are treated. The former city hall of an erstwhile bankrupt municipality is used as a hospital. There are only two private rooms and even these contain two beds. The rest is made up of a public ward for men and another for women. There is only one lavatory for the men and the same condition exists for the women. Those patients however are taken care of by specialists who reflect credit on our race.
The Quebec provincial government continues to turn a deaf ear to the reiterated requests of the medical profession which is loudly demanding a modern hospital. Hundreds of patients are waiting for their turn, due to a lack of space, and in the meantime their ailments get worse. And, in the case of cancer, a few weeks' delay in getting treated is enough to make the treatment useless and the disease incurable.
May I therefore be permitted to request the minister to grant to certain hospitals in our large centres the assistance required for the establishment of cancer clinics or simply to allow radium treatment for the patients. Let scholarships be given to our young doctors so that they may specialize in the large centres. Last year, more than 16,731 persons

died from cancerous diseases in Canada and among that number more than 500 were from the province of Quebec.
It is time to wage a relentless war against that disease to eradicate it, as was done in the case of tuberculosis. There again the provincial governments should get together with the federal government in order to put up a common front in this battle.

The government should spare no effort to facilitate the construction of houses if they do not want the country to face a few years hence a greater crisis than in 1945. Indeed in each of those areas industry is producing for this new defence department.

There are 6,000 members of these co-operatives and 1,200 only are house owners. All in all 120 new houses will be built at Cap-de-la-Madeleine as a result of this legislation.
I therefore ask the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) to facilitate the administration of this law, as far as the working class is concerned, by reducing the down payment. Mr. Speaker, there are just two other matters in connection with wheat I should like to emphasize at this time, before I go on to deal with the matter of farm income tax. We in this group were pleased indeed with the affirmative vote given by the Manitoba farmers in the plebiscite when they were asked whether they wished the Canadian wheat board to continue the marketing of coarse grains. Eighty-nine per cent of the farmers of Manitoba voted in favour of the wheat board method of marketing coarse grains. I feel confident that if such a vote were held in Saskatchewan we would do even better than the farmers of Manitoba, and would register a 95 per cent affirmative vote for the wheat board.
If western farmers believe so strongly in the wheat board method of marketing grain, then I say there is no longer any excuse, if indeed there ever was one, for the government allowing the grain exchange to stay open now and gamble in flax and rye. I say the grain exchange should be closed, and closed permanently, and the method by which it can be closed is for the government to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, as I hope it will, to include flax and rye under the operations of the wheat board. I feel

also the time has now come when the government should direct the wheat board to cease using the grain exchange in selling oats and barley. Through the Manitoba vote the farmers in western Canada have demonstrated that they are unalterably opposed to the grain exchange. Therefore the government should now place the marketing of all forms of grain exclusively under the Canadian wheat board.
I wish to say further, as I have already on a number of occasions this session, that the government cannot justifiably hold down to the international wheat agreement ceiling the price received by producers for domestic wheat. The international wheat agreement ceiling is now over 50 cents a bushel below the price received by the Canadian wheat board for class II wheat. The United States government gives the United States farmer the highest price, even though that government has to pay its farmers from the federal treasury as much as 73 cents a bushel on the wheat they produce. I say the very least the government of Canada can do is meet the request of the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the farmers' unions that the price of domestic wheat be increased at least to the extent of the increase in the farmers' cost of production.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the amendment, but in doing so I am not going to reply to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat because I think his words are answer enough to themselves. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) concerns a matter which has had considerable attention over a number of years. Some eight or nine years ago legislation was passed in the United States under which they pay up to 90 per cent of the floor price for grain stored on the farm. That has worked most successfully in getting deliveries of grain spread over a period of time rather than having it all rushed to market immediately after being threshed.
That has been one of our great difficulties In western Canada in the last two or three years, particularly when large crops have been harvested under adverse conditions resulting in a serious piling up of grain at both country and terminal elevators. This is due in large part to the fact that the grain is out of condition, and when grain is out of condition it takes more working space in
The Address-Mr. Wright both the country and terminal elevators in order to handle it. The result has been congestion all along the line.
As the hon. member for Assiniboia has said, last year we asked that a controller be appointed to relieve the situation, which was serious at that time. The government delayed taking action but finally did appoint a controller to relieve the congestion which existed this year. That controller has done a reasonably good job and has tried to keep grain moving. Last year the principal bottleneck was at the head of the lakes. Boats were not available for wheat carriage, being mainly engaged in the hauling of ore. Boats could not be obtained at the proper time to take the grain from the terminal elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William. Even with the best the controller has been able to do this year a serious situation still exists in western Canada. I have in my hand a report from the last issue of the Western Producer of November 29, which states:
